adjudicator: Opus (hand-adjudicated verse by verse; not a mechanical Isaiah collation — see the note below)
note: 3 Nephi 20 is one of the corpus's largest blocks of borrowing and it is NOT a transcribed Isaiah block in the sense of ADJUDICATING §5. It quotes Micah 5:8-9 and 4:12-13, then Acts 3:22-26 (and Deuteronomy 18 behind it), then Isaiah 52 in the order 8-10, 1-3, 6-7, 11-15 — out of sequence, so collate-isaiah.py's verse alignment cannot be used — and it rewrites what it quotes, replacing the LORD with the Father throughout the Isaiah portion and converting Peter's third-person sermon into the first person. Every verse was therefore collated by hand against its King James source and adjudicated individually. Hardy's convention of hanging a multi-verse citation on the LAST verse of the span it covers has been respected as a reading of his apparatus, not treated as a mis-keying: his rows at 20:17, 20:19, 20:35, 20:38, 20:40 and 20:45 each cover a span, and the catalogue writes a link at every verse in the span so that the differing degrees of alteration can be counted.

20:8.text: And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.

provenance.other: “never hunger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:35, where it stands in the same pair with “never thirst” that 3 Nephi 20:8 compresses into “never hunger nor thirst”. “drinketh my blood” occurs in exactly two, John 6:54 and John 6:56, and both couple it with eating, as this verse does. Revelation 7:16, “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more”, is the other candidate for the hunger-and-thirst clause and is displaced (see the exclusion register): it lacks the eating and drinking that occupy the first two thirds of the verse.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 26:26-27 supplies the narrative frame of verses 3-5 — took bread, blessed it, brake it, gave to the disciples — but not this verse's saying, which has no synoptic parallel. The Last Supper words are 'this is my body'; John 6's are 'he that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood'. 3 Nephi 20:8 has the second construction, not the first.
provenance.significance: The Fourth Gospel keeps its eucharistic discourse and its Last Supper apart: John 6 is preached in the synagogue at Capernaum a year early and John's supper narrative has no institution at all. 3 Nephi 20 puts them back together — the bread is broken and passed in verses 3-5, and then the Capernaum saying is spoken over it in verse 8. Recover John 6's context and what is recovered is the offence: 'This is an hard saying; who can hear it?' and 'from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him'. The saying that emptied the synagogue is here the saying over a meal at which the multitude is filled and cries out with one voice. The borrowing reverses the reception.

20:8.note: Not a quotation — no clause of John 6 is reproduced intact, and the verse falls far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold. The case is the collocation: eating a bread that is a body, drinking a drink that is blood, and a consequent hungering and thirsting no more, in that order, within one sentence. John 6 is the only KJV chapter where those three sit together. The 1830 reading is worth noticing on its own account: it reads 'eateth of my body to their soul … to their soul, and their soul shall never hunger', with a plural pronoun after the singular 'he that eateth', and 1920 regularized all three to 'his'. The first edition's grammar is looser than John's and than its own successor's.

20:13.text: And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south.

provenance.other: “from the east and from the west” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 107:3 and Luke 13:29. Psalm 107:3 is a gathering — 'And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south' — and 3 Nephi 20:13 is a gathering: 'shall the remnants … be gathered in from the east, and from the west, and from the south, and from the north'. Luke 13:29 is a banquet: those who 'come from the east, and from the west' sit down in the kingdom of God. The verb decides between them and it decides for the Psalm.
provenance.alternative: Luke 13:29 ranked first in the machine stream for this verse on a ten-word run and is filed in the exclusion register. Isaiah 43:5-6 has the same four quarters and the same gathering, but distributes them across two verses and four separate clauses ('I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west'), which is not this verse's shape.
provenance.significance: Whichever verse is in view, neither has the Book of Mormon's order. Psalm 107:3 and Luke 13:29 both run east, west, north, south; 3 Nephi 20:13 runs east, west, south, north. The transposition is the reason this row is moderate and not high, and it is worth recording rather than smoothing over, because the four-quarters gathering is a formula the Book of Mormon uses in its own right and a formula does not need a source.

20:13.note: A deliberately cautious row. The four compass points are common property and the catalogue does not claim otherwise; what makes the Psalm worth naming is that the pairing of the four quarters with the verb 'gather' is not common property — it is Psalm 107:3, and 3 Nephi 20:13 has both halves. Recorded at moderate so that a reader who arrives at this verse with Luke 13:29 in hand (as the machine did) is told which of the two verses actually shares the sense.
20:13.whyNot: The order of the quarters matches neither candidate, and 'gathered in from the four quarters' is a standing Book of Mormon idiom by this point in the text; the verse can be accounted for without any KJV verse at all.

20:16.text: And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles in the midst of many people as a lion among the beasts of the forest, as a young lion among the flocks of sheep: who, if he go through, both treadeth down, and teareth in pieces, and none can deliver.

provenance.other: “as a lion among the” and “none can deliver” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:8. “beasts of the forest” occurs in exactly two (Psalm 104:20, Micah 5:8) and “flocks of sheep” in exactly three (Genesis 29:2, Joel 1:18, Micah 5:8); only Micah 5:8 holds all four phrases, and 3 Nephi 20:16 has all four in Micah's order.
provenance.significance: The departures are all of one kind: Micah's third-person report becomes a second-person commission. Micah writes 'the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles'; the risen Christ says 'then shall ye, who are a remnant of the house of Jacob, go forth among them'. Micah's remnant is simply there among the nations, a lion by nature; 3 Nephi's is sent, and sent conditionally — verse 15 makes the whole sentence the apodosis of 'if the Gentiles do not repent'. So the one KJV verse in which Israel's remnant is a lion among the nations is here turned into a threat that repentance can still avert. Chapter 16 had already reached for this verse and reached for it in the negative (16:14-15, 'I will not suffer my people … to go through among them, and tread them down'); this is where the same verse is quoted almost whole.

20:16.note: Fifty-odd words tracking Micah 5:8 clause by clause, with four departures that all serve the change of person: 'the remnant of Jacob shall be' → 'ye, who are a remnant of the house of Jacob, go forth'; 'the Gentiles' → 'them' (Hardy's apparatus notes the substitution at this verse); 'in the midst of many people' → 'in the midst of them who shall be many'; and 'go through' → 'goeth through'. From 'as a lion' to 'none can deliver' — twenty-eight words — the verse is the King James Bible with one inserted conjunction. Well above Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though whether he counts it cannot be checked. Hardy hangs the citation for the whole span on the last verse of it, 20:17; the catalogue writes a link at each verse so that Micah 5:8 and 5:9 can be seen doing different work.

20:17.text: Thine hand shall be lifted up upon thine adversaries, and all thine enemies shall be cut off.

provenance.other: “lifted up upon thine adversaries” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:9. The verse is reproduced in full with a single word changed: the King James 'Thine hand' becomes 'Thy hand'. Everything after it — 'shall be lifted up upon thine adversaries, and all thine enemies shall be cut off' — is verbatim, and 'thine' survives twice in that stretch, so the change at the head of the verse is not a systematic modernization.
provenance.significance: The verse matters out of proportion to its length because of the two words at the end. 'Cut off' returns six verses later at 20:23, where it displaces Acts 3:23's 'destroyed' in the prophet-like-unto-Moses oracle, and Hardy's apparatus at 3 Nephi 21:11 observes that the term connects Deuteronomy 18:19 with Micah 5:8-15. The catalogue's own reading is that 3 Nephi 20 puts the connection into practice: it quotes Micah's cutting off here, and then, when it comes to Peter's sermon, it rewrites Peter with Micah's verb. The chapter's two great blocks of borrowing are stitched together at one word.

20:17.note: A sixteen-word verbatim reproduction, exactly at Skousen's threshold and therefore worth flagging for a reader collating this catalogue against his list; whether he counts it cannot be checked (PLAN §4.1). Hardy keys 'Verses 16-17 quote Mic 5.8-9' to this verse, which is his convention of hanging a multi-verse citation on the last member of the span; the wording of Micah 5:9 is genuinely here and nowhere else in the chapter.

20:18.text: But they know not the thoughts of the LORD, neither understand they his counsel: for he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor.

provenance.other: “sheaves into the floor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 4:12 — 'for he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor'. The threshing-floor image is common in the KJV; this particular collocation of sheaves with a floor and a gathering is not.
provenance.significance: Micah's simile has no agent inside it. 'He shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor' leaves the sheaves to arrive as sheaves do, and the point of the verse is that the nations gathered against Zion do not know they are being harvested. 3 Nephi supplies the missing farmer — 'as a man gathereth his sheaves into the floor' — and in doing so changes who is gathered. In Micah the sheaves are the hostile nations, brought in for threshing by the daughter of Zion in the next verse; in 3 Nephi 20:18 they are 'my people', gathered by their own God. The image survives the transfer intact and its referent is inverted, which is the same operation the chapter performs on Isaiah 52 twenty verses later.

20:18.note: Six shared words and one KJV singleton, which is what carries it; the departures are larger than the agreement. Catalogued at high rather than certain because the sentence is a paraphrase, not a quotation, and because a threshing-floor is available to any writer. What is not available to any writer is the sheaves-into-the-floor phrasing followed immediately, in the next verse, by the iron horn and brass hoofs of Micah 4:13 — the two verses arrive together and in Micah's order. Hardy keys 'Verses 18-19 quote Mic 4.12-13' to 20:19; this row puts the 4:12 half at the verse whose words it is.

20:19.text: Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion: for I will make thine horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass: and thou shalt beat in pieces many people: and I will consecrate their gain unto the LORD, and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth.

provenance.other: “thy hoofs brass”, “beat in pieces many people” and “consecrate their gain” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 4:13. “the Lord of the whole earth” occurs in exactly three (Psalm 97:5, Micah 4:13, Zechariah 4:14), and only Micah 4:13 has it in the same sentence as the other three. From 'I will make thy horn iron' to 'the Lord of the whole earth' the reproduction is verbatim but for 'thine horn' → 'thy horn'.
provenance.significance: What is dropped is the addressee. Micah 4:13 opens 'Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion' — Hardy's apparatus notes the missing clause — and 3 Nephi replaces it with 'I will make my people with whom the Father hath covenanted'. The daughter of Zion is displaced by a covenant people, and with her goes the imperative: Micah commands, 3 Nephi promises. The closing addition works the same way. Micah 4:13 ends with the substance consecrated to the Lord of the whole earth and no speaker named; 3 Nephi adds 'And behold, I am he who doeth it', which claims the whole oracle for the risen Christ standing in front of the crowd. Micah's verse is about what will be done; this one is about who is doing it.

20:19.note: Forty words of Micah 4:13, three KJV singletons among them, comfortably past Skousen's threshold. The 1830 running text carries a compositor's slip worth recording: it sets 'I will make thy hoops brass' where the King James reads 'hoofs', and later editions restore the source's word. The direction of that correction is the one CONVENTIONS §8 asks to be noticed — a later edition moving the Book of Mormon back toward the King James Bible rather than away from it — and it happens twice more in this chapter, at 20:42 and 20:45.

20:22.text: And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

provenance.other: “new Jerusalem” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 3:12 and Revelation 21:2, and in no Old Testament verse at all. Revelation 21:2 also supplies 'the holy city', which 3 Nephi 20 has fourteen verses later at 20:36 in its Isaiah 52:1 quotation — so both halves of Revelation's phrase are in this chapter, from two different directions.
provenance.alternative: Luke 21:26, 'the powers of heaven shall be shaken', is the only KJV verse containing 'powers of heaven' and therefore the highest-scoring candidate a rarity search returns for this verse. It is displaced in the exclusion register: Luke's powers are shaken in judgment and 3 Nephi's are present in blessing.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's New Jerusalem is not John's. Revelation 21:2 sees the city 'coming down from God out of heaven'; 3 Nephi 20:22 promises 'this people will I establish in this land … and it shall be a New Jerusalem', which locates it on the ground the audience is standing on. The borrowed phrase brings the whole eschatological weight of Revelation 21 with it and then spends that weight on a piece of American geography — the move the chapter has been making since verse 14, 'the Father hath commanded me that I should give unto you this land'.

20:22.note: Two words, and they would not be worth a row if they were two ordinary words. 'New Jerusalem' is a coinage of Revelation with no Old Testament ancestor, and a text purporting to be spoken by the risen Christ in the New World in the first century uses it as a known term needing no gloss. Recorded at moderate because the phrase is short enough to have been transmitted through ordinary nineteenth-century religious speech rather than off the page of Revelation, which is the standing difficulty with famous phrases. The rest of the verse — 'the powers of heaven shall be in the midst of this people; yea, even I will be in the midst of you' — has no verbal source the catalogue can identify; the nearest sense is Ezekiel 37:26-27 and Zechariah 2:10-11, and neither shares wording.

20:23.text: For Moses truly said unto the fathers, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you.

provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 18:15 — 'The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken.' Deuteronomy 18:19 — 'whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.'
provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15-19 → Acts 3:22-23 → KJV → Book of Mormon (with 1 Nephi 22:20 in between)
provenance.other: “raise up unto you of your brethren” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 3:22 and Acts 7:37, and in no Old Testament verse at all. mediation-check.py against Deuteronomy 18:15 and Acts 3:22 returns one decisive point and it is a sixteen-word one: the clause 'him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you' exists in Acts and not in Deuteronomy, and the Book of Mormon has it entire. Against Deuteronomy 18:19 and Acts 3:23 it returns two more, both decisive for Acts: 'every soul which' for Deuteronomy's 'whosoever', and 'hear that prophet' for Deuteronomy's 'hearken unto my words which he shall speak'. Acts 7:37 is displaced in the exclusion register — it stops at 'him shall ye hear' and cannot account for the twelve words that follow. The word order ('A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you') and the pronoun ('your God', not 'thy God') are Acts's throughout.
provenance.alternative: The one point at which this verse leaves Acts is its last verb: Acts 3:23 reads 'destroyed from among the people' and 3 Nephi 20:23 reads 'cut off from among the people'. That is precisely the departure 1 Nephi 22:20 had already made, in the same clause, five hundred pages earlier — so the proximate model for this one word is plausibly the earlier Book of Mormon rather than the King James Bible. It cannot be the model for the rest of the verse: 1 Nephi 22:20 omits 'of your brethren', and 3 Nephi 20:23 has it, which means the fuller Acts wording is independently in view. The schema carries a single mediation value and this row wants two; 'OT-via-NT' is recorded as the dominant route and the Book-of-Mormon-internal layer is stated here. FLAGGED for Wilson: a row with a genuinely double route has no clean representation in the field as defined.
provenance.significance: 'Cut off from among the people' occurs in no KJV verse. 'Cut off from among' occurs in eleven, and they are almost all Levitical: the karet formula, 'that soul shall be cut off from among his people', by which a violator is severed from Israel. So the substitution does not merely soften Peter's 'destroyed' — it exchanges an apostolic word for a priestly one, and re-files the penalty for refusing the prophet under the law of excommunication rather than of destruction. Hardy's apparatus observes at 3 Nephi 21:11 that 'cut off' is the term connecting Deuteronomy 18:19 with Micah 5:8-15; this chapter has just quoted Micah 5:9's 'all thine enemies shall be cut off' at 20:17, six verses back, which is where the catalogue thinks the verb was picked up.

20:23.note: A thirty-word run of Acts 3:22 followed by a seventeen-word run of Acts 3:23, with two departures: the introduction ('Behold, I am he of whom Moses spake, saying' for 'For Moses truly said unto the fathers') and the sanction ('cut off' for 'destroyed'). The first is the chapter's characteristic move — Peter's report of Moses becomes the speech of the one Moses spoke of, exactly as verses 24 and 26 turn Peter's 'these days' and 'his Son Jesus' into 'me'. The mediation is the same one the pilot got at 1 Nephi 22:20 and it is not close: the prophet-like-unto-Moses oracle reaches the Book of Mormon in Peter's wording, not Moses's. Well above Skousen's threshold; whether he counts it cannot be checked. Hardy cross-references Acts 3:23 and Deuteronomy 18:15, 18-19 here and notes both that Acts reads 'destroyed' and that 1 Nephi 22:20 also uses 'cut off'.

20:24.text: Yea, and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days.

provenance.other: “all the prophets from Samuel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:24. Eighteen consecutive words are reproduced without change — 'and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken' — and the verse departs only at its last five.
provenance.significance: Peter, preaching at Solomon's porch, says the prophets 'have likewise foretold of these days'; the speaker here says they 'have testified of me'. The change is small and it moves the referent of the entire prophetic tradition from an epoch to a person standing in front of the audience — and the person is the one Peter was preaching about. Verse 26 does the identical thing to Acts 3:26, where Peter's 'God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him' becomes 'the Father having raised me up … and sent me'. Read together, the three verses 23, 24 and 26 convert a sermon about Jesus into a sermon by him without altering the sermon.

20:24.note: The catalogue's claim here is narrow and checkable: eighteen words of Acts 3:24 in order, including a KJV singleton, with the closing clause replaced. Hardy cross-references Acts 3:24 at this verse and notes the divergent ending. Above Skousen's sixteen-word threshold on the unaltered stretch alone.

20:25.text: Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.

provenance.mt: Genesis 22:18 — 'And in thy seed shall all the NATIONS of the earth be blessed; BECAUSE THOU HAST OBEYED MY VOICE.'
provenance.route: Genesis 22:18 → Acts 3:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “kindreds of the earth be blessed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:25. mediation-check.py against Genesis 22:18 returns two decisive points, both for Acts: the Book of Mormon has 'kindreds', not Genesis's 'nations', and it stops where Acts stops, without Genesis's 'because thou hast obeyed my voice'. 'Children of the prophets' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 9:1 and Acts 3:25, and only Acts's are addressed to a congregation.
provenance.significance: The pronoun is the finding. Peter says the covenant was made 'with our fathers' — he is a Jew addressing Jews and includes himself. The speaker here says 'with your fathers', and the single letter changed is the whole difference between an Israelite preacher and the God of the covenant addressing Israel from outside the family. The same verse also converts Acts's 'God made' to 'the Father made', which is the substitution Hardy names as running through this discourse and which the Isaiah block at 20:32-35 performs on 'the LORD'. The catalogue's observation is that it begins here, eight verses earlier than the Isaiah quotation where it is usually noticed.

20:25.note: Seventeen consecutive words of Acts 3:25 at the close of the verse, and the Abrahamic promise reaches the Book of Mormon in Peter's form: 'kindreds', which is Acts's word for what Genesis calls nations. This is the fourth passage in the corpus to take Genesis 22:18 through Acts 3:25 rather than from Genesis (1 Nephi 15:18 and 22:9 are the earlier two, and 20:27 below is the second in this chapter), which makes Peter's sermon at Solomon's porch one of the most heavily used chapters in the New Testament for this text. Hardy cross-references Genesis 22:18 at this verse; the catalogue puts the link at Acts because that is the wording present.

20:26.text: Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities.

provenance.other: “turning away every one of you from his iniquities” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:26, and 3 Nephi 20:26 reproduces it word for word — thirteen consecutive words — along with 'unto you first', 'raised', 'sent' and 'to bless you' in Acts's order.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest instance in the chapter of a borrowing that is also a reattribution. Acts 3:26 is Peter speaking about a third party in the third person: 'Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you.' 3 Nephi 20:26 keeps every content word and moves the speaker: 'the Father having raised me up unto you first, and sent me to bless you.' God becomes the Father, his Son Jesus becomes me, and him becomes me — three substitutions, one operation. Nothing else in the sentence changes, which is why the operation is visible: the sermon is intact and only the person preaching it has moved.

20:26.note: A thirteen-word verbatim run inside a verse whose every other clause is Acts 3:26 recast into the first person. Below Skousen's threshold on the unaltered stretch, and that is the right way to read it — the length of the untouched clause is not the point, the systematic pronoun conversion is. Note that the conversion is not available to Peter and is not a paraphrase: it is the claim that the sermon Acts reports second-hand is here being delivered at first hand.

20:27.text: Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.

provenance.route: Genesis 22:18 → Acts 3:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “kindreds of the earth be blessed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:25. mediation-check.py at this verse returns the same two decisive points as at 20:25: 'kindreds' for Genesis's 'nations', and the absence of Genesis's closing 'because thou hast obeyed my voice'. The promise is quoted here as a twelve-word run, 'In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed'.
provenance.significance: A second citation of the same clause two verses after the first is not a narrator reusing his own formula, which is the case ADJUDICATING §4 sends to the exclusion register; it is a speaker quoting a text twice in order to argue from it twice. At 20:25 the promise establishes who the audience is — 'ye are of the covenant which the Father made with your fathers'. At 20:27 the same words are made to run forward instead of backward: 'after that ye were blessed, then fulfilleth the Father the covenant … unto the pouring out of the Holy Ghost through me upon the Gentiles.' The seed in which all kindreds are blessed is first the audience's ancestry and then, on the second reading, the mechanism by which the blessing leaves them for the Gentiles and returns as a scourge. Abraham's promise is the hinge of the chapter's whole argument about scattering and gathering, and it is quoted twice because it has to face both ways.

20:27.note: The row is written rather than sent to the exclusion register as a within-book repeat because the repetition is the argument, in the sense ADJUDICATING §4 ratified at Mosiah 29:2 — the second use answers the first rather than reiterating it. The wording is Acts's, not Genesis's, on the same two tests that decided 20:25.

20:32.text: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion.

provenance.other: “see eye to eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:8. The middle of the verse — 'with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye' — is verbatim; the frame is rewritten at both ends. Isaiah's 'Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice' becomes 'Then shall their watchmen lift up their voice', and Isaiah's closing 'when the LORD shall bring again Zion' is dropped and replaced by the whole of the next verse.
provenance.alternative: This is the fourth time the corpus quotes Isaiah 52:8 (Mosiah 12:22, Mosiah 15:29, 3 Nephi 16:18) and the possibility of an OT-via-earlier-BoM mediation has to be taken seriously, because 'their voice' agrees with Mosiah 15:29 against Isaiah 52:8, Mosiah 12:22 and 3 Nephi 16:18, which all read 'the voice'. Two things hold the catalogue back from recording that route. First, 3 Nephi 20:32 recasts the whole verse into the third person ('their watchmen', 'Then shall'), and once the watchmen are theirs the voice follows without any need of a model. Second, Hardy's apparatus records a possible reading 'the voice' at this verse and at Mosiah 15:29 alike — so the single word on which the earlier-Book-of-Mormon case rests is textually unsettled at both ends of the comparison. The mediation is recorded as direct-OT and the condition that would overturn it is stated: if 'their' is the reading at both places, this row should become OT-via-earlier-BoM.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's watchmen sing when the LORD brings again Zion; the clause is the reason they sing. 3 Nephi cuts it and replaces it with 'Then will the Father gather them together again, and give unto them Jerusalem' (20:33) — which keeps Isaiah's 'again' and exchanges Zion for Jerusalem and the LORD for the Father. Chapter 16 had quoted this verse whole and unaltered eight chapters earlier. Setting 16:18 beside 20:32 gives the clearest single view in the Book of Mormon of the difference between transcribing Isaiah and interpreting him, because the same speaker does both to the same verse.

20:32.note: Fourteen verbatim words of Isaiah 52:8 inside a verse whose opening and closing clauses are rewritten. Below Skousen's threshold on the unbroken run, and the row is not about length: Hardy's own note at 20:35 is that this second quotation carries 'interpretive variations' where the earlier one at 3 Nephi 16:18-20 was very close to the King James Bible, and the point of cataloguing all four members of the block at 20:32-35 separately is to let each variation be seen. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:8 at this verse and records a possible reading 'the voice' for the text's 'their voice'.

20:33.text: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion.

provenance.other: No phrase of Isaiah 52:8 survives here except the adverb. Isaiah's clause is 'when the LORD shall bring again Zion'; this verse is 'Then will the Father gather them together again, and give unto them Jerusalem for the land of their inheritance'. Of Isaiah's six words, one is retained — 'again' — and it is retained in a different construction.
provenance.significance: The verse is the clearest place in the chapter to watch the substitution Hardy names operating on more than a divine title. Three things change at once: the LORD becomes the Father, bringing again becomes gathering together again, and Zion becomes Jerusalem given as a land of inheritance. The third is the substantive one. Isaiah's clause is about a city restored to itself; 3 Nephi's is about a people restored to a territory, which is the vocabulary the chapter has used since verse 14 ('this land, for your inheritance') and will use again at its last words in verse 46 ('it shall be the land of their inheritance'). Isaiah's closing clause is not dropped; it is translated into the chapter's own idiom of covenant land.

20:33.note: Recorded at high confidence and low verbal scores, which is the shape CONVENTIONS §3 exists to allow: the dependence is not seriously deniable, because this verse occupies exactly the position in the Isaiah 52:8-10 sequence that the excised clause vacated, and yet almost no wording is shared. Hardy attaches Isaiah 52:8 to this verse with the note that Isaiah reads 'when the Lord shall bring again Zion' — that is, he records the reference precisely as a replacement, which is how the catalogue reads it too.
20:33.whyNot: One shared word. Anybody proposing this link from verbal evidence alone would be wrong to; it rests entirely on sequence and on the clause it displaces.

20:34.text: Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the LORD hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “break forth into joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:9, and so does “waste places of Jerusalem”. From 'sing together' to 'he hath redeemed Jerusalem' the verse is verbatim but for one word: 'the LORD hath comforted his people' becomes 'the Father hath comforted his people'.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 49:13, 'break forth into singing, O mountains: for the LORD hath comforted his people', is the other KJV verse joining a breaking forth to that clause and is displaced in the exclusion register; it has neither the joy nor the waste places.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:9 is an imperative addressed to ruins: break forth, sing, because the comforting has already happened. 3 Nephi turns the first half into a prediction — 'Then shall they break forth into joy' — and leaves the second half as Isaiah's imperative, so the verse is half foretold and half commanded, and the seam falls exactly where the chapter's own frame ends and the quotation begins. The comforting is then reassigned: the LORD who comforted his people in Isaiah is the Father here, which is the substitution running through 20:32-35 and, as 20:25 shows, through the Acts block before it. Compare 3 Nephi 16:19, where the same verse stands with no alteration at all.

20:34.note: Twenty-two words of Isaiah 52:9 with a single word replaced, past Skousen's threshold on the unbroken stretch. The value of the row is comparative: the catalogue already holds this verse unaltered at 3 Nephi 16:19 and at Mosiah 12:23 and 15:30, so the one word changed here is measurable against three earlier copies rather than only against the King James Bible.

20:35.text: The LORD hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

provenance.other: “made bare his holy arm”, “in the eyes of all the nations” and “ends of the earth shall see” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:10 — three singletons in twenty-five words. The two departures are both at the divine names: 'The LORD hath made bare' → 'The Father hath made bare', and 'the salvation of our God' → 'the salvation of the Father'. “I and my Father are one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:30, and the appended clause 'and the Father and I are one' is that verse with its two terms reversed.
provenance.significance: Chapter 16 removed a word here and chapter 20 fills the hole. At 3 Nephi 16:20 Isaiah's 'the salvation of our God' was quoted as 'the salvation of God', with the possessive simply deleted and nothing put in its place; here the possessive is supplied, and supplied as 'the Father'. Then the sentence does not stop where Isaiah stops. It adds 'and the Father and I are one', which is John 10:30 inverted, and the addition is what makes the whole substitution legible: if the Father and the speaker are one, then replacing Isaiah's LORD with the Father through four verses has changed the reference of nothing. The chapter rewrites Isaiah's divine name and then, in five words, argues that the rewriting was not a change. Hardy directs the reader to 3 Nephi 11:27 at this point, where the same unity is stated of Father, Son and Holy Ghost.

20:35.note: Twenty-five words of Isaiah 52:10 carrying three KJV singletons, two divine-name substitutions, and a five-word Johannine addition. Well past Skousen's threshold. Hardy hangs 'Verses 32-35 quote Isa 52.8-10' on this verse, notes that this is the second time the speaker quotes the passage, and observes that the earlier wording at 3 Nephi 16:18-20 was very close to the King James Bible whereas here the original Lord is replaced by Father throughout — which is the sentence that governs how this whole block has been adjudicated. The catalogue writes four links rather than one so that the replacement can be counted verse by verse.

20:36.text: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.

provenance.other: “put on thy beautiful garments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:1, and so does “the uncircumcised and the unclean”. Apart from two inserted words the verse is reproduced entire — thirty consecutive words from 'put on thy strength, O Zion' to 'the uncircumcised and the unclean'. The insertion is 'again, and': 'Awake, awake again, and put on thy strength'.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 52:1-2 had already been quoted in the corpus at 2 Nephi 8:24-25, inside the Isaiah 51-52 block, and an OT-via-earlier-BoM route has to be weighed. At this verse it is not supported: 2 Nephi 8:24 reads 'Awake, awake, put on thy strength' with the King James Bible, and 3 Nephi 20:36's 'again, and' is this verse's own. The following verse, 20:37, gives a different answer.
provenance.significance: 'Awake, awake again' is not a stutter. Isaiah 52:1 is itself a second awakening — it answers Isaiah 51:9's 'Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD' and 51:17's 'Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem', so the chapter opens by waking a city that has been told to wake twice already. The inserted 'again' says out loud what Isaiah's arrangement implies, which is a small but real piece of interpretation performed inside a quotation. Note also where the quotation begins: this chapter reached Isaiah 52 at verse 8 first (20:32, and 3 Nephi 16:18 before that), and only now goes back for the opening. The frame is quoted after the middle, which is why the verse order of the block runs 8-10, 1-3, 6-7, 11-15.

20:36.note: A thirty-word verbatim run, comfortably past Skousen's threshold, in a verse the corpus has quoted once before. Hardy keys 'Verses 36-38 quote Isa 52.1-3' to 20:38 and notes that Isaiah 52:1-2 was also quoted at 2 Nephi 8:24-25; the catalogue writes a link at each of 36, 37 and 38 because the three verses stand in three different relations to the earlier Book of Mormon quotation.

20:37.text: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:2 → KJV → 2 Nephi 8:25 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “captive daughter of Zion” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:2, and so does “the bands of thy neck”. The verse is otherwise reproduced entire, seventeen consecutive words at the end of it, with exactly one departure from the King James Bible: Isaiah reads 'arise, AND sit down, O Jerusalem' and 3 Nephi 20:37 reads 'arise, sit down, O Jerusalem'.
provenance.alternative: A dropped conjunction is thin evidence for a route on its own, and two writers could drop it independently. What makes it worth recording is that it is the ONLY departure in either passage: 2 Nephi 8:25 reproduces Isaiah 52:2 word for word except for the same missing 'and', and 3 Nephi 20:37 reproduces it word for word except for the same missing 'and'. Two verbatim quotations of one verse, made hundreds of pages apart, agreeing in their single deviation. Both readings hold in the 1830, 1920 and current editions, so this is not an artifact of the running text chosen. Compare 20:36, where 2 Nephi 8:24 and 3 Nephi 20:36 do NOT agree — 3 Nephi adds 'again, and' where 2 Nephi has the King James text — which is the control that keeps this from being a claim about the block as a whole.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's cleanest instance of the route CONVENTIONS §7 predicted would appear from 2 Nephi onward: a Book of Mormon passage whose proximate model is an earlier Book of Mormon passage rather than the Bible. The evidence is a single conjunction, which is exactly the kind of evidence a mediation test is built to use — the pilot's sixteen OT-via-NT rows each turned on one word. The metaleptic payoff is that the chapter is quoting a text its audience's own scriptures already contained: Nephi had read Isaiah 52:1-2 to this people's ancestors six centuries earlier, and the risen Christ gives it back to them in the form their own record preserved.

20:37.note: Seventeen words verbatim and one conjunction missing, and the missing conjunction carries the row. Past Skousen's threshold on run length. The mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM with its evidence stated in full above so that a reader who thinks one dropped 'and' is too little can see exactly what the claim rests on and decline it. Hardy notes at 20:38 that Isaiah 52:1-2 was also quoted at 2 Nephi 8:24-25; the collation of the two Book of Mormon passages against each other, and the finding, are the catalogue's own.
20:37.whyNot: One word, and a function word at that. If 2 Nephi 8:25's omission and 3 Nephi 20:37's omission are independent — and a light conjunction is the likeliest word in the verse to drop by accident twice — the route collapses to direct-OT and nothing else in the verse would notice.

20:38.text: For thus saith the LORD, Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.

provenance.other: “sold yourselves for nought” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:3, and so does “redeemed without money”. The verse is reproduced without a single substantive change — eighteen consecutive words — the only difference being the printing of 'the Lord' for the King James small-capital 'LORD', which is a compositor's choice and not a reading.
provenance.significance: The verse is worth its row precisely because nothing happens to it. Isaiah 52 reaches this chapter under continuous alteration — the LORD becomes the Father at 20:34 and 20:35, the watchmen change person at 20:32, an 'again' is inserted at 20:36, a conjunction is dropped at 20:37 — and then verse 3 arrives untouched. It is also the one verse of the quoted portion that speaks of a redemption without payment, which the chapter has no need to reassign, since the speaker is the redeemer. Where the substitutions stop is as much a fact about the discourse as where they occur.

20:38.note: Eighteen words verbatim, two KJV singletons, above Skousen's threshold. The 1830 sets 'nought', the King James spelling, where later editions read 'naught' — one of three places in this chapter (with 'hoofs' at 20:19 and 'rereward' at 20:42) where the first edition preserves the source's orthography and a later edition modernizes it. CONVENTIONS §8's first bullet, three times in one chapter. Hardy keys 'Verses 36-38 quote Isa 52.1-3' to this verse.

20:39.text: Therefore my people shall know my name: therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I.

provenance.other: “he that doth speak” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:6. The shared material is substantial — 'my people shall know my name', 'they shall know', 'in that day', 'that I am he that doth speak' — but reordered: Isaiah has 'they shall know in that day that I am he', and 3 Nephi has 'in that day they shall know that I am he'. Isaiah's two 'therefore's are replaced by 'Verily, verily, I say unto you' and 'yea', and Isaiah's closing three words are dropped.
provenance.significance: What is dropped is the point. Isaiah 52:6 ends 'behold, it is I' — a self-identification deferred to a future day when the people will at last know the name. The speaker of 3 Nephi 20 removes it, and he removes it because he has just supplied it in person: the chapter opened with the multitude giving glory to Jesus 'whom they both saw and heard' (20:9). Isaiah's promise that one day they will know that I am he that doth speak is quoted by the one speaking, to people who are looking at him. The excision is the fulfilment. Hardy's apparatus records the missing clause without comment; the reading of it is the catalogue's.

20:39.note: Substantial verbal agreement with one KJV singleton, but the clause order is rearranged and the verse is framed by the Book of Mormon's own 'Verily, verily, I say unto you', so it falls below Skousen's threshold on any single unbroken run. Certain nonetheless: Isaiah 52:6 is the only verse in the Bible with this combination, and it arrives in the exact sequential position between the block's 52:3 and 52:7. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:6 here and quotes the omitted words.

20:40.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “how beautiful upon the mountains” and “Thy God reigneth” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:7; “that publisheth peace” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15. mediation-check.py against Romans 10:15 and Nahum 1:15 returns seven decisive points and every one favours Isaiah: the Book of Mormon has 'How beautiful' where Nahum has 'Behold', keeps 'that publisheth salvation … Thy God reigneth' which Nahum lacks entirely, and keeps 'bringeth good tidings, that publisheth' where Romans reads 'preach the gospel of'. The only departure from Isaiah is a twice-inserted 'unto them' after 'good tidings'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:7 is the most quoted verse of this chapter in the New Testament — Paul cites it at Romans 10:15 to argue that the gospel must be preached before it can be believed — and the mediation test is decisive that it does not reach 3 Nephi through Paul. That is worth stating because the context here is Paul's context: verse 30 has just promised that 'the fulness of my gospel shall be preached unto them', which is Romans 10's argument exactly, and the quotation that follows is still Isaiah's wording and not Paul's. The doubled 'unto them' is the interpretive addition: Isaiah's herald brings good tidings to nobody in particular, and here the tidings have an addressee — the scattered Israel of verse 29 to whom the gospel is to be preached.

20:40.note: Thirty-odd words tracking Isaiah 52:7 clause for clause with two identical two-word insertions, well past Skousen's threshold on the unbroken stretches. The verse has been quoted twice before in the corpus, at Mosiah 12:21 and in Abinadi's exposition at Mosiah 15:14-18, neither of which has the doubled 'unto them'; so unlike 20:37, this verse gives no evidence of an earlier-Book-of-Mormon route. Hardy keys 'Verses 39-40 quote Isa 52.6-7' to this verse and notes the Mosiah quotations.

20:41.text: Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD.

provenance.other: “bear the vessels of the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:11. The verse is otherwise reproduced whole, eighteen consecutive words from 'go ye out of the midst of her' to the end, with one clause rephrased: Isaiah's 'touch no unclean thing' becomes 'touch not that which is unclean'.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 6:17 quotes this verse — 'come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing' — and the Book of Mormon's 'touch not' agrees with Paul's negative against Isaiah's 'touch no'. mediation-check.py nonetheless returns three decisive points for Isaiah and none for Paul: the Book of Mormon has 'Depart ye, depart ye, go ye' where Paul has 'Wherefore come', keeps 'from thence' which Paul lacks, and keeps the whole of 'go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the Lord', for which Paul substitutes 'and I will receive you'. The mediation is direct-OT; the rephrased clause is filed in the exclusion register so that a reader who notices the agreement with Paul is told the catalogue noticed it too.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:11 is addressed to the priests carrying the temple vessels out of Babylon, and the uncleanness it forbids is the ritual kind — a thing, an object one might handle on the road. 'Touch not that which is unclean' loosens the object into a category, which is the direction 2 Corinthians 6:17 had already taken the verse when Paul made it about company rather than cargo. So the departure moves with the New Testament's reading without adopting the New Testament's words — the sense is Pauline and the vocabulary is Isaian. That combination is worth recording precisely because the mediation test says it is not a case of borrowing from Paul.

20:41.note: Eighteen words verbatim, past Skousen's threshold, inside a verse whose only alteration is a four-word rephrasing and an added frame ('And then shall a cry go forth'). Hardy keys 'Verses 41-45 quote Isa 52.11-15' to 20:45, his convention of hanging the citation on the last verse of a span; the catalogue writes a link at each of the five so that the very different amounts of alteration in them can be seen. He also notes at 3 Nephi 21:29 that the speaker there returns to Isaiah 52:11 and to this verse.

20:42.text: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the LORD will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward.

provenance.other: “nor go by flight” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:12, and “will be your rereward” in exactly one, the same verse. The whole verse is reproduced — twenty-four consecutive words — with a single word changed: 'the God of Israel WILL be your rereward' becomes 'SHALL be your rereward'.
provenance.significance: One auxiliary verb, and it is the same auxiliary the chapter has been putting into Isaiah since verse 32. Isaiah's futures are statements about what God will do; 3 Nephi's are promises inside a covenant being enacted in front of an audience, and 'shall' is the covenanting form. The metalepsis is in what Isaiah 52:12 is doing when it says it: the verse contrasts the return from Babylon with the Exodus, where Israel DID go out in haste (Exodus 12:11, 'ye shall eat it in haste'). Quoted here, the promise of an unhurried departure with God before and behind is addressed to a people whose founding story in this book is a hurried flight from Jerusalem.

20:42.note: Twenty-four words verbatim with one auxiliary changed, past Skousen's threshold. The 1830 keeps the King James spelling 'rereward' — an archaic form of rearguard, which Hardy has to gloss for his own readers — and 1920 modernizes it to 'rearward'. The first edition therefore shows the borrowing on the page in a way the current text does not, which is the whole reason CONVENTIONS §8 makes the 1830 the running text.

20:43.text: Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high.

provenance.other: “exalted and extolled” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:13, as do “deal prudently” and “my servant shall deal”. The verse is reproduced entire and without any change whatever — sixteen consecutive words, the whole verse.
provenance.significance: This is where the Book of Mormon's most consequential piece of Isaiah interpretation begins, and it begins by changing nothing. Isaiah 52:13-15 opens the fourth Servant Song, which runs on into Isaiah 53; the speaker here quotes its first three verses verbatim at 20:43-45 and then, in the next chapter, takes them up as a prophecy of a latter-day servant and of a book (21:8-11, where Hardy notes that the 'marred' of Isaiah 52:14 is applied to a named individual). So the exact reproduction here is the precondition for the reading there: the text has to be given whole before it can be reapplied.

20:43.note: A sixteen-word verbatim reproduction of an entire verse, three KJV singletons in it, and exactly at Skousen's threshold — worth flagging for anyone collating this catalogue against his list of long quotations, though whether he counts it cannot be checked (PLAN §4.1). Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:13-14 and this verse at 3 Nephi 21:10, which is where the servant passage is put to work.

20:44.text: As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men:

provenance.other: “his visage was so marred” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:14. Twenty consecutive words are reproduced from 'his visage' to 'the sons of men'. The single departure is the opening participle: Isaiah reads 'As many were ASTONIED at thee', and 3 Nephi 20:44 reads 'astonished'.
provenance.alternative: “astonished at thee” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Ezekiel 26:16, 27:35 and 28:19 — and Isaiah 52:14 is not among them, so a rarity search on the Book of Mormon's own wording lands on the oracles against Tyre rather than on the Servant Song. That is a trap and it is filed in the exclusion register. Nothing else in the verse is Ezekiel's, and the twenty words after the participle are Isaiah's alone.
provenance.significance: 'Astonied' is the King James Bible's older form and it occurs in ten of its verses; 'astonished' is the form that displaced it, and every edition of the Book of Mormon from 1830 onward has the modern word. It is the only place in this chapter's whole Isaiah block where the Book of Mormon reads a modernization of the King James vocabulary rather than preserving it — and it stands three verses after 'rereward', which the 1830 preserves and 1920 modernizes. The two words pull in opposite directions within a single page, which is a useful caution against treating the first edition's relation to the King James Bible as uniform.

20:44.note: Twenty words verbatim past a single modernized participle, well above Skousen's threshold. The one substituted word is the row's whole interest, because it is a substitution of exactly the kind CONVENTIONS §8 says to watch for and it runs the other way from the chapter's other three. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:13-14 at 3 Nephi 21:10.

20:45.text: So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.

provenance.other: “sprinkle many nations” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:15, and so does “shut their mouths”. The verse is reproduced entire. In the current and 1920 texts there is no departure at all; in the 1830 running text there is exactly one, and it is an omitted negative.
provenance.significance: The 1830 sets 'for that which had been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider', dropping the 'not' from the first clause and keeping it in the second. Isaiah's couplet depends on both negatives — kings fall silent because what was never reported to them is now in front of their eyes — and without the first one the line says the opposite of what the second says, which is why later editions restore it. This is CONVENTIONS §8's second pattern and the clearest instance the catalogue has met: a first-edition reading that departs from the King James Bible, and a later edition correcting the Book of Mormon back TOWARD its source. The chapter contains three such corrections — 'hoops' to 'hoofs' at 20:19, this omitted negative, and, running the other way, 'rereward' to 'rearward' at 20:42.

20:45.note: A complete verbatim verse in the modern text, past Skousen's threshold; the finding is in the 1830. The missing negative also matters downstream, because 3 Nephi 21:8 quotes the second half of this verse again — 'kings shall shut their mouths; for that which had not been told them shall they see' — and the 1830 prints the 'not' there, so the first edition disagrees with itself about the same clause one chapter apart. Hardy keys 'Verses 41-45 quote Isa 52.11-15' to this verse and cross-references 20:45 from 21:8.

20:46.text: In that day will I make the governors of Judah like an hearth of fire among the wood, and like a torch of fire in a sheaf; and they shall devour all the people round about, on the right hand and on the left: and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again in her own place, even in Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “inhabited again” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Zechariah 12:6 — 'and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again in her own place, even in Jerusalem'. 3 Nephi 20:46 reads 'then shall Jerusalem be inhabited again with my people'. The shared material is 'Jerusalem … be inhabited again', four words plus the name, and the name is in both clauses in the same syntactic slot. “shall be inhabited” occurs in exactly four KJV verses and only Zechariah 12:6 has the adverb.
provenance.significance: Zechariah 12 is the chapter in which Jerusalem is besieged by all nations and delivered, and its reinhabitation is the reward for a siege survived. 3 Nephi 20 ends on the same note and reaches it by an entirely different route — through a covenant with Abraham, a scattering by the Gentiles and a gathering by the Father. The borrowed adverb carries Zechariah's premise with it: 'again' presumes an emptying, and the chapter has spent forty-five verses describing one. Note too what the chapter does with 'in her own place'. Zechariah insists the restored city is the old city on the old ground; 3 Nephi 20:46 replaces that clause with 'with my people … and it shall be the land of their inheritance', which is the covenant-land vocabulary of 20:14 and 20:33.

20:46.note: A row the machine did not propose and that a reader could reasonably decline. Four shared words is very little, and 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited' is a thought a writer on the restoration of Israel might have without a source. What lifts it to moderate is that the adverb is a KJV singleton and that it is the operative word in both sentences — in Zechariah because the city was emptied, here because the people were scattered. Recorded under CONVENTIONS §0a as a connection worth gesturing at; declining it costs the catalogue nothing and it is offered on that understanding.
20:46.whyNot: Four words, one of them a proper noun. There is no syntactic agreement beyond the phrase itself, no second point of contact anywhere in the verse, and the wider contexts share a topic rather than a text.
